Polynomials Counting Group Colorings in Graphs

Houshan Fu

School of Mathematics and Information Science

Guangzhou University

Guangzhou 510006, Guangdong, P. R. China

Email: fuhoushan@gzhu.edu.cn

Abstract

Jaeger et al. in 1992 introduced group coloring as the dual concept to group connectivity in graphs. Let AA be an additive Abelian group, f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A and DD an orientation of a graph GG. A vertex coloring c:V⁡(G)→Ac:V(G)\to A is an (A,f)(A,f)-coloring if c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​ve=uv from uu to vv under DD. Kochol recently introduced the assigning polynomial to count nowhere-zero chains in graphs–nonhomogeneous analogues of nowhere-zero flows in [17], and later extended the approach to regular matroids in [18]. Motivated by Kochol’s work, we define the α\alpha-compatible graph and the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) at kk in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs, where α\alpha is an assigning of GG from its cycles to {0,1}\{0,1\}. We prove that P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) evaluates the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings of GG for any Abelian group AA of order kk and f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A such that the assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} given by ff equals α\alpha. Such an assigning is admissible. Based on Kochol’s work, we derive that k−c⁡(G)​P​(G,α,k)k^{-c(G)}P(G,\alpha;k) is a polynomial enumerating (A,f)(A,f)-tensions and counting specific nowhere-zero chains.

Furthermore, by extending Whitney’s broken cycle concept to broken compatible cycles, we show that the absolute value of the coefficient of k|V⁡(G)|−ik^{|V(G)|-i} in P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) associated with admissible assignings α\alpha equals the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that have ii edges and contain no broken α\alpha-compatible cycles. According to the combinatorial explanation, we establish a unified order-preserving relation from admissible assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials, and further show that for any admissible assigning α\alpha of GG with α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1 for every loop ee, the coefficients of P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) are nonzero and alternate in sign.

Keywords: Graph coloring, tension, chromatic polynomial, assigning polynomial, α\alpha-compatible graph, broken cycle


Mathematics Subject Classifications: 05C31, 05C15

1 Introduction

The graphs GG with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G) considered in this paper are finite, allowing multiple edges and loops. A more general setting and background on graphs can be found in the book [5]. An orientation of a graph is an assignment of direction to each edge. In this context, each oriented edge is referred to as an arc. An oriented graph arises from a graph GG together with a particular orientation DD, denoted by D⁡(G):=(V⁡(D),A⁡(D))D(G):=\big(V(D),A(D)\big), where V⁡(D)=V⁡(G)V(D)=V(G) and A⁡(D)A(D) is the collection of arcs under the orientation DD.

Graph coloring is a significant subfield in graph theory that originated in the middle of the 19th century with the famous Four Color Problem. A kk-vertex coloring of GG is a mapping c:V⁡(G)→Sc:V(G)\to S, where SS is a set of distinct kk colors, typically S={1,2,…,k}S=\{1,2,...,k\}. A vertex coloring cc is proper if c⁡(u)≠c⁡(v)c(u)\neq c(v) whenever vertices uu and vv are adjacent.

We consider a finite additive Abelian group AA with the identity 00 as coloring sets in this paper. Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi [14] introduced the concept of group coloring as the dual concept of group connectivity of graphs in 1992. Group connectivity and group colorings of graphs are nicely surveyed in [21]. Let f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A be a function. A vertex coloring c:V⁡(G)→Ac:V(G)\to A is called an (A,f)(A,f)-coloring if c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​ve=uv from uu to vv under an orientation DD of GG. When f≡0f\equiv 0, (A,0)(A,0)-coloring is exactly the ordinary proper coloring. Furthermore, GG is said to be AA-colorable under the orientation DD if for any function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A, GG always admits an (A,f)(A,f)-coloring. Since then, topics related to group coloring problems have attracted a lot of research attentions, such as [19, 26, 27, 28, 20, 22, 23, 25]. Their primary focus is on the (weak) group chromatic number and related group coloring problems, such as whether a graph that is A1A_{1}-colorable for some Abelian group A1A_{1} is also A2A_{2}-colorable for any Abelian group A2A_{2} of the same order. However, another fundamental problem of counting (A,f)(A,f)-colorings has been overlooked. In this paper, we introduce the cycle-assigning polynomial, a concept inspired by Kochol’s work [17, 18], which precisely counts the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings of graphs and generalizes the classical chromatic polynomial. We primarily investigate its fundamental properties, particularly focusing on its coefficients.

A fundamental problem in graph theory is determining the chromatic number of a graph, which refers to the smallest integer kk such that the graph admits a proper coloring with kk colors. Counting proper colorings can be seen as another facet of this problem. In an attempt to address the long-standing Four Color Problem, Birkhoff [3] discovered that the number of proper colorings of a planar GG with kk colors is a polynomial in kk, known as the chromatic polynomial. Whitney [36, 37] later extended the concept of the chromatic polynomial to general graphs and gave a combinatorial description of its coefficients by introducing the broken cycle, now famously known as the Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem. Since then, various generalizations of this theorem have been developed across different mathematical structures, such as matroids [6, 10], lattices [4, 32], hyperplane arrangements [29], hypergraphs [8]. See [9] for more related work. Motivated by these work, it is natural to ask the two questions:

  • •

    Is there a polynomial function of |A||A| that generalizes the chromatic polynomial and counts (A,f)(A,f)-colorings in graphs?

  • •

    Can we provide a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of the polynomial function?

It is worth remarking that the difference between the Abelian group colorings of vertices in an oriented graph gives rise to a group-valued function on arcs, refereed to as a tension, whose value at each arc is the head-point value minus the tail-point value of the coloring. From this perspective, the proper colorings correspond to nowhere-zero tensions. It is known that the number of nowhere-zero tensions in Abelian groups of orders kk is also a polynomial. This was first introduced by Tutte [34] and later formally named the tension polynomial of GG by Kochol [15]. Note that the tension polynomial is a nontrivial divisor of the chromatic polynomial. For more related work, refer to [7, 16]. Likewise, an arbitrary (A,f)(A,f)-coloring of GG also produces an (A,f)(A,f)-tension, whose detailed definition will be formally presented in Section 3. Naturally, there are two questions regarding (A,f)(A,f)-tensions analogous to the aforementioned ones in (A,f)(A,f)-colorings. An answer to the first question in (A,f)(A,f)-tensions seems to be implicit in the work of Kochol [18]. We shall present an explicit answer to this question in Corollary 3.2, and further explore the connection between (A,f)(A,f)-colorings and nowhere-zero chains related to homomorphisms (see [18]) in Section 3.

To answer these questions, several significant works should be noted. Most recently, Kochol [17] first introduced the assigning polynomial to count nowhere-zero chains in graphs–nonhomogeneous analogues of nowhere-zero flows (called (A,b)(A,b)-flows in [24]) by the zero-one assigning from certain vertex sets of GG to the set {0,1}\{0,1\}, which is a generalization of the classical flow polynomial [34]. Subsequently, Kochol [18] further extended the approach for represented regular matroids to count nowhere-zero chains associated with homomorphisms and zero-one assignings from circuits of a regular matroid to {0,1}\{0,1\}. Kochol’s pioneering work has been a cornerstone of our research. Particularly, the zero-one assignings on cycles of graphs play a central role in the study of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings and (A,f)(A,f)-tensions in graphs.

A cycle CC of GG is a connected 2-regular subgraph of GG. The corresponding edge set E⁡(C)E(C) is referred to as a circuit of GG. Let 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) be the family of cycles of GG. An assigning of GG is a mapping from 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) to {0,1}\{0,1\}. Write α≡0\alpha\equiv 0 if α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all C∈𝒞⁡(G)C\in\mathcal{C}(G) or 𝒞⁡(G)=∅\mathcal{C}(G)=\emptyset.

To more conveniently investigate the properties of the cycle-assigning polynomials, we use the α\alpha-compatible graph to mirror the role of both the (M,≺)(M,\prec)-compatible and δ⁡(M,α,X)\delta(M,\alpha;X) associated with a matroid MM introduced by Kochol [18] (see Section 3 for detailed definitions).

Definition 1.1.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of a graph GG. GG is said to be α\alpha-compatible if α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for its every cycle CC. A subgraph HH of GG is called an α\alpha-compatible subgraph if the restriction of α\alpha to HH satisfies α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all cycles CC in HH. In this sense, HH is αH\alpha_{H}-compatible, where αH\alpha_{H} is the restriction of α\alpha to HH defined by αH​(C):=α​(C)\alpha_{H}(C):=\alpha(C) for any cycle CC of HH.

We first provide an explicit formula for the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings via the α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph expansion in Theorem 2.1. Inspired by this expression, we define a cycle-assigning polynomial in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs. As shown in Theorem 2.2, this polynomial precisely count (A,f)(A,f)-colorings of graphs.

Definition 1.2.

For any assigning α\alpha of GG, the cycle-assigning polynomial of GG is defined as

P⁡(G,α,k):=∑H is an α-compatiblespanning subgraph of G(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H),P(G,\alpha;k):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mbox{$H$ is an $\alpha$-compatible}\\ \mbox{spanning subgraph of $G$}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)},

where c⁡(H)c(H) is the number of components of HH.

Furthermore, let

τ⁡(G,α,k):=∑H is an α-compatiblespanning subgraph of G(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kr⁡(G)−r⁡(H),\tau(G,\alpha;k):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mbox{$H$ is an $\alpha$-compatible}\\ \mbox{spanning subgraph of $G$}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{r(G)-r(H)},

where r⁡(H):=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(H)r(H):=|V(G)|-c(H). To better distinguish both polynomials P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) and τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k), we call τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) an α\alpha-assigning polynomial of GG originating from [17, 18]. It should be noted that the (A,f)(A,f)-tension serves as a bridge connecting (A,f)(A,f)-colorings and nowhere-zero chains associated with regular matroids and homomorphisms (see Section 3 for detailed discussion).

Due to Kochol’s work [17, 18], we show that τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) not only enumerates (A,f)(A,f)-tensions of GG but also counts the number of certain nowhere-zero chains in AE⁡(G)A^{E(G)}, as stated in Corollary 3.2. As a direct consequence of [18, Theorem 2], an alternative expression for P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) and τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) is presented in Corollary 3.6.

To address the second question, we extend the broken cycle [36] to the broken α\alpha-compatible cycle. In Theorem 4.2, we show that the unsigned coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials associated with admissible assignings α\alpha can be expressed in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that do not contain broken α\alpha-compatible cycles. This generalizes the Whitney’s celebrated Broken Cycle Theorem [36]. Accordingly, we establish a unified order-preserving relation from admissible assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials when both are naturally ordered in Theorem 5.1. Additionally, we provide a new perspective on solving group coloring problems in graphs, with detailed discussion in Section 5.

Notice that the α\alpha-assigning polynomial τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) is a nontrivial divisor of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k), that is, P⁡(G,α,k)=kc⁡(G)​τ​(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=k^{c(G)}\tau(G,\alpha;k). Thus, the coefficients of τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) share the same properties as those of P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k).

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 is devoted to studying the counting function for the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings and the cycle-assigning polynomial. In Section 3, we mainly explain the close connection between cycle-assigning polynomials and Kochol’s work [18]. In Section 4 and Section 5, we focus on exploring the properties of coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials associated with admissible assignings.

2 Cycle-assigning polynomials

In this section, we focus on the study of cycle-assigning polynomials, exploring their structural properties and their roles in counting (A,f)(A,f)-colorings. Let us review some necessary notations and definitions on graphs. Throughout this paper, we always denote by SES^{E} the collection of mappings from a finite set EE to a set SS, unless otherwise stated. The elements of SES^{E} are considered as vectors indexed by EE. An edge with identical ends is called a loop, and an edge with distinct ends is a link. A graph HH is a subgraph of GG if V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(H)⊆E⁡(G)E(H)\subseteq E(G). When V⁡(H)=V⁡(G)V(H)=V(G), the subgraph HH of GG is referred to as a spanning subgraph. For an edge subset S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G), G−SG-S is the spanning subgraph obtained by removing the edges in SS. Denote by G|SG|S the spanning subgraph with edges SS, that is, G|S=G−(E⁡(G)∖S)G|S=G-(E(G)\smallsetminus S). Conversely, if HH is a proper subgraph which does not contain the edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G) with both ends of ee are in V⁡(H)V(H), then we denote by H+eH+e the subgraph of GG by adding the edge ee to HH. In addition, if ee is a link of GG, the graph G/eG/e is obtained by contracting ee, that is, identifying the ends of ee to create a single new vertex and then removing ee. Note that even the graph GG is simple, the contraction G/eG/e may not be simple, and repeated contractions may also result in loops.

Unless otherwise stated, we always choose an arbitrary but fixed reference orientation DD for GG. Notice that every cycle CC of GG has exactly two possible directions. We arbitrarily choose and fix a direction o⁡(C)o(C) for every cycle CC. Associated with each cycle CC of GG, the orientation DD of GG induces a map ηD⁡(C)\eta_{D(C)} from the edge set E⁡(G)E(G) to the set {0,±1}\{0,\pm 1\} defined by

ηD⁡(C)​(e):={1,if e∈E⁡(C), the direction of e is consistent with o⁡(C);−1,if e∈E⁡(C), the direction of e is opposite to o⁡(C);0,if e∈E⁡(G)∖E⁡(C).\eta_{D(C)}(e):=\begin{cases}1,&\mbox{if $e\in E(C)$, the direction of $e$ is consistent with $o(C)$};\\ -1,&\mbox{if $e\in E(C)$, the direction of $e$ is opposite to $o(C)$};\\ 0,&\mbox{if $e\in E(G)\smallsetminus E(C)$}.\end{cases} (2.1)

Remarkably, each function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A automatically induces an assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} on 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) such that for each cycle CC of GG,

αD,f​(C):={0, if ​∑e∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0;1, otherwise.\alpha_{D,f}(C):=\begin{cases}0,&\mbox{ if }\sum_{e\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0;\\ 1,&\mbox{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

We say that α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f} is DD-admissible, or simply admissible.

Although, the map ηD⁡(C)\eta_{D(C)} induced by a cycle CC depends on the arbitrarily chosen direction of CC, different directions of CC only cause a possible −1-1 factor to the ηD⁡(C)\eta_{D(C)} value on each edge of CC. Thus, whether ∑e∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)\sum_{e\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e) equals 00 is independent of the choice of direction of CC. Consequently, the choice of direction for cycles has no influence on the assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f}, and hence does not affect our results.

To derive an explicit formula for the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings, the Möbius Inversion Formula in [5, Theorem 2.25] is needed. It is stated that if the function g:2E⁡(G)→Ag:2^{E(G)}\to A is defined as

g⁡(S):=∑S⊆X⊆E⁡(G)h⁡(X) for ∀S⊆E⁡(G),g(S):=\sum_{S\subseteq X\subseteq E(G)}h(X)\quad\mbox{ for }\quad\forall\,S\subseteq E(G),

then, for all S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G),

h⁡(S)=∑S⊆X⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|X|−|S|​g​(X),h(S)=\sum_{S\subseteq X\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|X|-|S|}g(X), (2.2)

where hh is a function from the family 2E⁡(G)2^{E(G)} of all edge subsets of GG to AA.

Let f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A, and P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)P\big(D(G),f;A\big) denote the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings of GG under DD. The result below shows that P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)P\big(D(G),f;A\big) can be expanded in terms of αD,f\alpha_{D,f}-compatible spanning subgraphs.

Theorem 2.1 (Counting Formula).

Let f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A and α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}. Then

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑H is an α-compatiblespanning subgraph of G(−1)|E⁡(H)|​|A|c⁡(H).P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mbox{$H$ is an $\alpha$-compatible}\\ \mbox{spanning subgraph of $G$}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}|A|^{c(H)}.
Proof.

For any S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G), let CS​(D​(G),f,A)C_{S}\big(D(G),f;A\big) be the number of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Ac:V(G)\to A such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S from uu to vv, and PS​(D​(G),f,A)P_{S}\big(D(G),f;A\big) be the number of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Ac:V(G)\to A such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S and c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​v∈E⁡(G)∖Se=uv\in E(G)\smallsetminus S. We have

CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A)=CS​(D⁡(G),f,A),P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=P∅​(D⁡(G),f,A)C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big)=C_{S}\big(D(G),f;A\big),\quad\quad P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=P_{\emptyset}\big(D(G),f;A\big)

and

C∅​(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)PS​(D⁡(G),f,A).C_{\emptyset}\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}P_{S}\big(D(G),f;A\big).

It follows from (2.2) that

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A).P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big). (2.3)

In [15, Proposition 2.2], it is demonstrated that GG admits a vertex coloring cc such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for any oriented edge e=u​ve=uv of GG if and only if ff satisfies the condition ∑e∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0 for every cycle CC of GG. This is further equivalent to α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all cycles CC of GG since α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}. Thus, CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A)=0C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big)=0 whenever G|SG|S is an α\alpha-incompatible subgraph of GG. Then, P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)P\big(D(G),f;A\big) in (2.3) is simplified to the form

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑S⊆E⁡(G),G|S​ is αG|S-compatible(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A).P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq E(G),\\ G|S\mbox{ is $\alpha_{G|S}$-compatible}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big). (2.4)

Denote by CS​(D⁡(G)|S,fS;A)C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f_{S};A\big) the collection of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Ac:V(G)\to A of G|SG|S such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each oriented edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S. Then, fixing a vertex coloring c∈CS​(D⁡(G)|S,fS;A)c\in C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f_{S};A\big), every vertex coloring c′∈CS​(D⁡(G)|S,fS;A)c^{\prime}\in C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f_{S};A\big) gives rise to a unique vertex coloring c′−c∈CS​(D⁡(G)|S,0S;A)c^{\prime}-c\in C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,0_{S};A\big). Conversely, every vertex coloring c′′∈CS​(D⁡(G)|S,0S;A)c^{\prime\prime}\in C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,0_{S};A\big) also gives rise to a unique vertex coloring c+c′′∈CS​(D⁡(G)|S,fS;A)c+c^{\prime\prime}\in C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f_{S};A\big). Notice

CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A)=|CS​(D⁡(G)|S,fS;A)| and CS​(D⁡(G)|S,0;A)=|CS​(D⁡(G)|S,0S;A)|.C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big)=|C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f_{S};A\big)|\quad\mbox{\rm~and~}\quad C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,0;A\big)=|C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,0_{S};A\big)|.

It follows that

CS​(D⁡(G)|S,f;A)=CS​(D⁡(G)|S,0;A)=|A|c⁡(G|S).C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,f;A\big)=C_{S}\big(D(G)|S,0;A\big)=|A|^{c(G|S)}.

Together with (2.4), we have

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=∑S⊆E⁡(G),G|S​ is αG|S-compatible(−1)|S|​|A|c⁡(G|S),P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq E(G),\\ G|S\mbox{ is $\alpha_{G|S}$-compatible}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S|}|A|^{c(G|S)},

which completes the proof. ∎

As a direct consequence of Theorem 2.1, the cycle-assigning polynomials corresponding to admissible assignings precisely count the number of (A,f)(A,f)-colorings of GG.

Theorem 2.2.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG. Then P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)P(G,\alpha;k)=P\big(D(G),f;A\big) for every orientation DD of GG, every Abelian group AA of order kk and every function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A satisfying αD,f=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha.

By applying Theorem 2.2, we immediately obtain the following corollary. This implies that the number of (G,f)(G,f)-colorings depends only on the assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f}, and not on the structure of AA and the choice of the orientation DD.

Corollary 2.3.

Let D,D′D,D^{\prime} be distinct orientations of GG, and A,A′A,A^{\prime} be two Abelian groups of the same order and functions f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A, f′:E⁡(G)→A′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to A^{\prime}. If αD,f=αD′,f′\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}}, then P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=P⁡(D′​(G),f′,A′)P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};A^{\prime}\big).

We further explore the fundamental properties of cycle-assigning polynomials. Suppose e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G) is a link of GG. Then the set 𝒞⁡(G/e)\mathcal{C}(G/e) of cycles of G/eG/e consists of two parts:

𝒞−e(G):={C∈𝒞(G/e)∩𝒞(G):e∉E(C)},𝒞/e(G/e):={C/e:C∈𝒞(G),e∈E(C)}.\mathcal{C}_{-e}(G):=\big\{C\in\mathcal{C}(G/e)\cap\mathcal{C}(G):e\notin E(C)\big\},\;\mathcal{C}_{/e}(G/e):=\big\{C/e:C\in\mathcal{C}(G),e\in E(C)\big\}.

In this context, each assigning α\alpha of GG induces an assigning αG/e\alpha_{G/e} of G/eG/e, where αG/e​(C):=α​(C)\alpha_{G/e}(C):=\alpha(C) for C∈𝒞−e​(G)C\in\mathcal{C}_{-e}(G) and αG/e​(C/e):=α⁡(C)\alpha_{G/e}(C/e):=\alpha(C) for C∈𝒞⁡(G)C\in\mathcal{C}(G) containing ee. If ee is a loop of GG, then 𝒞⁡(G−e)=𝒞⁡(G/e)⊆𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G-e)=\mathcal{C}(G/e)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(G). In this case, each assigning α\alpha of GG naturally induces assignings αG−e\alpha_{G-e} of G−eG-e and αG/e\alpha_{G/e} of G/eG/e, where αG−e​(G)​(C)=αG/e​(C):=α⁡(C)\alpha_{G-e}(G)(C)=\alpha_{G/e}(C):=\alpha(C) for each C∈𝒞⁡(G−e)C\in\mathcal{C}(G-e).

Next, we introduce a fundamental property concerning admissible assignings.

Lemma 2.4.

Let α\alpha be a DD-admissible assigning of GG, TT be a spanning forest of GG and fT:E⁡(T)→Af_{T}:E(T)\to A. Then there exists a function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A such that αD,f=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha and f​(e)=fT​(e)f(e)=f_{T}(e) for any e∈E⁡(T)e\in E(T).

Proof.

Since α\alpha is a DD-admissible assigning of GG, there exists a function g:E⁡(G)→Ag:E(G)\to A such that αD,g=α\alpha_{D,g}=\alpha. For each edge e∈E⁡(G)∖E⁡(T)e\in E(G)\smallsetminus E(T), let CeC_{e} be the unique cycle (fundamental cycle) in the spanning subgraph T+eT+e. Define a new function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A as follows:

f⁡(e)={fT​(e), if ​e∈E⁡(T);∑h∈E⁡(Ce)ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​g​(h)−∑h∈E⁡(Ce)∖{e}ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​fT​(h), if ​e∈E⁡(G)∖E⁡(T).f(e)=\begin{cases}f_{T}(e),&\text{ if }e\in E(T);\\ \sum_{h\in E(C_{e})}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)g(h)-\sum_{h\in E(C_{e})\smallsetminus\{e\}}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)f_{T}(h),&\mbox{ if }e\in E(G)\smallsetminus E(T).\end{cases}

Consequently, for any e∈E⁡(G)∖E⁡(T)e\in E(G)\smallsetminus E(T), we have

∑h∈E⁡(Ce)ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​f​(h)=∑h∈E⁡(Ce)ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​g​(h).\sum_{h\in E(C_{e})}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)f(h)=\sum_{h\in E(C_{e})}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)g(h).

In [5, Corollary 4.11], it is demonstrated that every cycle CC of GG can be expressed uniquely as a symmetric difference of fundamental cycles CeC_{e} for all e∈E⁡(C)∖E⁡(T)e\in E(C)\smallsetminus E(T). This implies that

ηD⁡(C)=∑e∈E⁡(C)∖E⁡(T)δC,Ce​ηD⁡(Ce),\eta_{D(C)}=\sum_{e\in E(C)\smallsetminus E(T)}\delta_{C,C_{e}}\eta_{D(C_{e})},

where δC,Ce=1\delta_{C,C_{e}}=1 if the direction of ee is either consistent with or opposite to both o⁡(C)o(C) and o⁡(Ce)o(C_{e}), and δC,Ce=−1\delta_{C,C_{e}}=-1 otherwise. Therefore, for every cycle CC of GG, we have

∑h∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(h)​f​(h)\displaystyle\sum_{h\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(h)f(h) =∑h∈E⁡(C)∑e∈E⁡(C)∖E⁡(T)δC,Ce​ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​f​(h)\displaystyle=\sum_{h\in E(C)}\sum_{e\in E(C)\smallsetminus E(T)}\delta_{C,C_{e}}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)f(h)
=∑e∈E⁡(C)∖E⁡(T)δC,Ce​∑h∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​f​(h)\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(C)\smallsetminus E(T)}\delta_{C,C_{e}}\sum_{h\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)f(h)
=∑e∈E⁡(C)∖E⁡(T)δC,Ce​∑h∈E⁡(Ce)ηD⁡(Ce)​(h)​g​(h)\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(C)\smallsetminus E(T)}\delta_{C,C_{e}}\sum_{h\in E(C_{e})}\eta_{D(C_{e})}(h)g(h)
=∑h∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(h)​g​(h).\displaystyle=\sum_{h\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(h)g(h).

It follows that αD,f=αD,g=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D,g}=\alpha. This completes the proof. ∎

We now present a deletion-contraction formula for cycle-assigning polynomials, which provides an inductive approach to proving the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem (see Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 2.5 (Deletion-contraction Formula).

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG. For any e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), αG−e\alpha_{G-e} and αG/e\alpha_{G/e} are admissible assignings of G−eG-e and G/eG/e, respectively, and

P⁡(G,α,k)={k|V⁡(G)|, if ​E​(G)=∅;k−1k​P​(G−e,αG−e,k), if ​e​ is a bridge;α⁡(e)​P​(G−e,αG−e,k), if ​e​ is a loop;P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)−P⁡(G/e,αG/e,k), otherwise.P(G,\alpha;k)=\begin{cases}k^{|V(G)|},&\mbox{ if }E(G)=\emptyset;\\ \frac{k-1}{k}P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\mbox{ if }e\mbox{ is a bridge};\\ \alpha(e)P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\mbox{ if }e\mbox{ is a loop};\\ P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)-P(G/e,\alpha_{G/e};k),&\mbox{ otherwise}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Clearly, αG−e\alpha_{G-e} is admissible for any e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), and αG/e\alpha_{G/e} is admissible if ee is a loop. When ee is a link, from Lemma 2.4, we can choose a function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A such that αD,f=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha and f⁡(e)=0f(e)=0. Then αG/e=αD,f−e\alpha_{G/e}=\alpha_{D,f_{-e}}, where f−ef_{-e} is the restriction of ff to E⁡(G)∖{e}E(G)\smallsetminus\{e\}. Consequently, αG/e\alpha_{G/e} is admissible .

Let 𝒮e\mathcal{S}_{e} be the family of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing ee and 𝒮−e\mathcal{S}_{-e} be the family of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain ee. If ee is a bridge, then a subgraph HH containing ee is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG if and only if H−eH-e is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG. Therefore, we conclude that every α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG containing ee gives rise to a unique α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph H−eH-e of GG that does not contain ee, and vice versa. Then we have

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H+e)|​kc⁡(H+e)+∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H+e)|}k^{c(H+e)}+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}.

Since ee is a bridge, c⁡(H+e)=c⁡(H)−1c(H+e)=c(H)-1 for any H∈𝒮−eH\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}. Hence, we deduce

P⁡(G,α,k)=k−1k​P​(G−e,αG−e,k).P(G,\alpha;k)=\frac{k-1}{k}P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k).

If ee is a loop, we need to consider both cases: α⁡(e)=0\alpha(e)=0 and α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1. For the former case, similarly to the case where ee is a bridge, we can easily derive P⁡(G,α,k)=0P(G,\alpha;k)=0. For the latter case, it is clear that HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG if and only if HH is an αG−e\alpha_{G-e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−eG-e. So, we arrive at P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k).

If ee is neither a bridge nor a loop, then HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no ee if and only if HH is an αG−e\alpha_{G-e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−eG-e, and HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing ee if and only if H/eH/e is an αG/e\alpha_{G/e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G/eG/e. Therefore, we have

P⁡(G,α,k)\displaystyle P(G,\alpha;k) =∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)+∑H∈𝒮e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)\displaystyle=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}
=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)+∑H∈𝒮e(−1)|E⁡(H/e)|+1​kc⁡(H/e)\displaystyle=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(-1)^{|E(H/e)|+1}k^{c(H/e)}
=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)−P⁡(G/e,αG/e,k),\displaystyle=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)-P(G/e,\alpha_{G/e};k),

which completes the proof. ∎

In addition, the general cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) has the following simple decomposition formula.

Theorem 2.6.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and G=G1⊔G2⊔⋯⊔GiG=G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup G_{i}, where GjG_{j} is the component of GG for j=1,2,…,ij=1,2,\ldots,i. Then

P⁡(G,α,k)=∏j=1iP⁡(Gj,αGj,k).P(G,\alpha;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{i}P(G_{j},\alpha_{G_{j}};k).
Proof.

Since GG decomposes into the union of the components GjG_{j} of GG, each α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG is partitioned into the disjoint union of the αGj\alpha_{G_{j}}-compatible spanning subgraph of GjG_{j}, and vice versa. Therefore, we have P⁡(G,α,k)=∏j=1iP⁡(Gj,αGj,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{i}P(G_{j},\alpha_{G_{j}};k). ∎

At the end of the section, we list the cycle-assigning polynomials for the empty graph, a tree and the cycle on nn vertices.

Example 2.7.

Note that the following assignings are admissible obviously.

  • (1)

    Let OnO_{n} be the empty graph on nn vertices. Then α≡0\alpha\equiv 0 and

    P⁡(On,0,k)=kn.P(O_{n},0;k)=k^{n}.
  • (2)

    Let TnT_{n} be a tree on nn vertices. Then α≡0\alpha\equiv 0 and

    P⁡(Tn,0,k)=k​(k−1)n−1=∑i=1n(−1)n−i​(n−1i−1)​ki.P(T_{n},0;k)=k(k-1)^{n-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}\binom{n-1}{i-1}k^{i}.
  • (3)

    Let CnC_{n} be a cycle on nn vertices. Combining part (2) and Theorem 2.5, we have

    P⁡(Cn,α,k)={(k−1)n+(−1)n​(k−1), if ​α​(Cn)=0;(k−1)n+(−1)n+1, if ​α​(Cn)=1.P(C_{n},\alpha;k)=\begin{cases}(k-1)^{n}+(-1)^{n}(k-1),&\mbox{ if }\alpha(C_{n})=0;\\ (k-1)^{n}+(-1)^{n+1},&\mbox{ if }\alpha(C_{n})=1.\end{cases}

3 Polynomials counting nowhere-zero chains associated with homomorphisms

In this section, we mainly clarify the close relationship between cycle-assigning polynomials and α\alpha-assigning polynomials, which was first introduced by Kochol [17] to count nowhere-zero chains in graphs–nonhomogeneous analogues of nowhere-zero flows. Most recently, Kochol [18] further extended the approach to regular matroids. For this purpose, we first review some basic definitions about regular chain groups associated to regular matroids. For additional properties of regular chain groups, refer to the references [2, 35].

A regular matroid M=M⁡(U)M=M(U) on a ground set EE is represented by a totally unimodular matrix UU. A more general setting and background on matroids can be found in Oxley’s book [30]. A chain on EE over an Abelian group AA is a map f∈AEf\in A^{E}, and its support σ⁡(f)\sigma(f) is σ⁡(f):={f⁡(e)≠0∣e∈E}\sigma(f):=\{f(e)\neq 0\mid e\in E\}. We say that ff is proper if σ⁡(f)=E\sigma(f)=E. Associated with UU or M⁡(U)M(U), a regular chain group NN on EE over ℤ\mathbb{Z} is the set of integral vectors orthogonal to each row of UU. The set of chains orthogonal to every chain of NN forms a chain group called orthogonal to NN, denoted by N⟂N^{\perp}. Actually, N⟂N^{\perp} consists of the integral vectors from the linear combinations of the rows of UU. A chain ff of NN is elementary if there is a no nonzero chain gg of NN such that σ⁡(g)⊂σ⁡(f)\sigma(g)\subset\sigma(f). An elementary chain ff of NN is said to be primitive if f⁡(e)∈{±1,0}f(e)\in\{\pm 1,0\} for all e∈Ee\in E. In this section, we always assume that a regular chain group NN is associated with a totally unimodular matrix U⁡(N)U(N) representing a regular matroid M=M⁡(N)M=M(N).

Let AA be an additive Abelian group. We shall consider AA as a (right) ℤ\mathbb{Z}-module such that the scalar multiplication a⋅za\cdot z of a∈Aa\in A by z∈ℤz\in\mathbb{Z} equals zero if z=0z=0, ∑1za\sum_{1}^{z}a if z>0z>0, and ∑1−z(−a)\sum_{1}^{-z}(-a) if z<0z<0. Analogously, if a∈Aa\in A and f∈ℤEf\in\mathbb{Z}^{E}, then define a⋅f∈AEa\cdot f\in A^{E} such that (a⋅f)​(e)=a⋅f​(e)(a\cdot f)(e)=a\cdot f(e) for every e∈Ee\in E. We shall denote by A⁡(N)A(N) the AA-chain group generated by the regular chain group NN, that is,

A(N):={∑i=1mai⋅fi∣ai∈A,fi∈N,m≥1}.A(N):=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\cdot f_{i}\mid a_{i}\in A,f_{i}\in N,m\geq 1\Big\}.

Let A⁡[N]A[N] be the collection of all proper AA-chains from A⁡(N)A(N), i.e.,

A⁡[N]:={f∈A⁡(N)∣σ⁡(f)=E}.A[N]:=\big\{f\in A(N)\mid\sigma(f)=E\big\}.

From [2, Proposition 1], we have

g∈AE​ is from ​A​(N)⟺∑e∈Eg⁡(e)⋅f⁡(e)=0​ for any ​f∈N⟂.g\in A^{E}\text{ is from }A(N)\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{e\in E}g(e)\cdot f(e)=0\text{ for any }f\in N^{\perp}. (3.1)

Let ψ\psi be a homomorphism from a regular chain group NN to AA. Define by

Aψ​[N]:={g∈(A−0)E∣∑e∈Eg⁡(e)⋅f⁡(e)=ψ⁡(f)​ for all ​f∈N}.A_{\psi}[N]:=\Big\{g\in(A-0)^{E}\mid\sum_{e\in E}g(e)\cdot f(e)=\psi(f)\text{ for all }f\in N\Big\}.

Each element from Aψ​[N]A_{\psi}[N] is called a proper (N,ψ)(N,\psi)-chain.

Let 𝒫⁡(N)\mathcal{P}(N) be the set of primitive chains of a regular chain group NN, and 𝒞⁡(M)\mathcal{C}(M) be the family of circuits of M=M⁡(N)M=M(N). By [35], 𝒫⁡(N)\mathcal{P}(N) and 𝒞⁡(M)\mathcal{C}(M) have the following relationship

𝒞⁡(M)={σ⁡(c)∣c∈𝒫⁡(N)}.\mathcal{C}(M)=\big\{\sigma(c)\mid c\in\mathcal{P}(N)\big\}. (3.2)

An assigning of MM is any mapping α\alpha from 𝒞⁡(M)\mathcal{C}(M) to {0,1}\{0,1\}. Write α≡0\alpha\equiv 0 if α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all C∈𝒞⁡(M)C\in\mathcal{C}(M) or 𝒞⁡(M)=∅\mathcal{C}(M)=\emptyset. Let e∈Ee\in E. It follows from the relation 𝒞⁡(M−e)⊆𝒞⁡(M)\mathcal{C}(M-e)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(M) that an assigning α\alpha of MM naturally gives rise to an assigning α⁡[−e]\alpha[-e] of M−eM-e for which

α⁡[−e]​(C)=α⁡(C),C∈𝒞⁡(M−e).\alpha[-e](C)=\alpha(C),\quad C\in\mathcal{C}(M-e).

By [30, Proposition 3.1.10], we know that

if C∈𝒞⁡(M/e)C\in\mathcal{C}(M/e), then either C∈𝒞⁡(M)C\in\mathcal{C}(M) or C∪e∈𝒞⁡(M)C\cup e\in\mathcal{C}(M).

Similarly, the assigning α\alpha of MM also induces an assigning α[/e]\alpha[/e] of M/eM/e such that α[/e](C)=α(C)\alpha[/e](C)=\alpha(C) if C∈𝒞⁡(M/e)∩𝒞⁡(M)C\in\mathcal{C}(M/e)\cap\mathcal{C}(M), and α[/e](C)=α(C∪e)\alpha[/e](C)=\alpha(C\cup e) otherwise.

From (3.2), the homomorphism ψ\psi automatically leads to an assigning αN,ψ\alpha_{N,\psi} of MM such that for every c∈𝒫⁡(N)c\in\mathcal{P}(N),

αN,ψ​(σ⁡(c)):={0,if ​ψ​(c)=0;1,if ​ψ​(c)≠0.\alpha_{N,\psi}\big(\sigma(c)\big):=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }\psi(c)=0;\\ 1,&\text{if }\psi(c)\neq 0.\end{cases}

An assigning α\alpha of MM is said to be homogeneous if there exists a homomorphism ψ:N→A\psi:N\to A such that α=αN,ψ\alpha=\alpha_{N,\psi}. Furthermore, ψ\psi and α=αN,ψ\alpha=\alpha_{N,\psi} are proper if Aψ​[N]≠∅A_{\psi}[N]\neq\emptyset.

In 2024, Kochol showed in [17, Theorem 1] that there exists a polynomial p⁡(M,α,k)p(M,\alpha;k) counting the number of nowhere-zero chains in Aψ​[N]A_{\psi}[N]. The polynomial p⁡(M,α,k)p(M,\alpha;k) is called an α\alpha-assigning polynomial of MM by Kochol.

Theorem 3.1 ([18], Theorem 1).

Suppose MM is a regular matroid on EE and α\alpha is a homogeneous assigning of MM. Then, there exists a polynomial p⁡(M,α,k)p(M,\alpha;k), such that p⁡(M,α,k)=|Aψ​[N]|p(M,\alpha;k)=|A_{\psi}[N]| for every regular chain group NN on EE and M⁡(N)=MM(N)=M, every Abelian group AA of order kk, and every homomorphism ψ:N→A\psi:N\to A satisfying αN,ψ=α\alpha_{N,\psi}=\alpha. If α\alpha is proper, then p⁡(M,α,k)p(M,\alpha;k) has degree r⁡(M)r(M), and p⁡(M,α,k)=0p(M,\alpha;k)=0 otherwise. Furthermore, for any e∈Ee\in E, α⁡[−e]\alpha[-e] and α[/e]\alpha[/e] are homogeneous assignings of M−eM-e and M/eM/e, respectively, and

p⁡(M,α,k)={1,if E=∅;(k−1)​p​(M−e,α⁡[−e],k),if e is a bridge;α⁡(e)​p​(M−e,α⁡[−e],k),if e is a loop;p(M−e,α[−e];k)−p(M/e,α[/e];k),otherwise.p(M,\alpha;k)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $E=\emptyset$};\\ (k-1)p\big(M-e,\alpha[-e];k\big),&\text{if $e$ is a bridge};\\ \alpha(e)p\big(M-e,\alpha[-e];k\big),&\text{if $e$ is a loop};\\ p\big(M-e,\alpha[-e];k\big)-p\big(M/e,\alpha[/e];k\big),&\text{otherwise}.\\ \end{cases}

Below we shall explore some applications of the α\alpha-assigning polynomial to colorings and tensions of GG. The incidence matrix of D⁡(G)D(G) is the |V⁡(D)|×|A⁡(D)||V(D)|\times|A(D)| matrix MD⁡(G):=(mv​a)M_{D(G)}:=(m_{va}) whose rows and columns are indexed by the vertices and arcs, where, for a vertex vv and arc aa

mv​a:={1, if arc ​a​ is a link and vertex ​v​ is the head of ​a;−1, if arc ​a​ is a link and vertex ​v​ is the tail of ​a;0, otherwise.m_{va}:=\begin{cases}1,&\text{ if arc }a\text{ is a link and vertex }v\text{ is the head of }a;\\ -1,&\text{ if arc }a\text{ is a link and vertex }v\text{ is the tail of }a;\\ 0,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

If c∈AV⁡(G)c\in A^{V(G)}, then the coboundary of cc is the map δ​c∈AE⁡(G)\delta c\in A^{E(G)} given by

δ​c​(e):=∑v∈V⁡(G)mv​D​(e)​c​(v),\delta c(e):=\sum_{v\in V(G)}m_{vD(e)}c(v),

where D⁡(e)D(e) denotes the corresponding arc of the edge ee under DD. In this sense, we call a mapping t∈AE⁡(G)t\in A^{E(G)} a tension or an AA-tension if there exists a vertex coloring c∈AV⁡(G)c\in A^{V(G)} such that t=δ​ct=\delta c. Similar to (A,f)(A,f)-coloring associated with a mapping f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)}, a tension tt is referred to as an (A,f)(A,f)-tension if it satisfies t⁡(e)≠f⁡(e)t(e)\neq f(e) for all e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G). In particular, taking f≡0f\equiv 0, the (A,0)(A,0)-tension is exactly the nowhere-zero AA-tension. It is clear that all AA-tensions form an (additive) Abelian subgroup of AE⁡(G)A^{E(G)}, denoted by Δ⁡(G,A)\Delta(G,A). Let Δf​(G,A)\Delta_{f}(G,A) be the set of all (A,f)(A,f)-tensions of GG for f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)}. The number of nowhere-zero tensions is evaluated by a polynomial τ⁡(G,k)\tau(G;k) in kk introduced by Tutte [34]. This was developed and formally named the tension polynomial of GG by Kochol [15] in 2002. Motivated by their work, a natural question arises:

  • •

    Is there a polynomial function of |A||A| that generalizes the tension polynomial and counts (A,f)(A,f)-tensions in graphs?

The answer to the question was implicit in the work of Kochol [18]. By applying Theorem 3.1, we shall present an explicit answer in Corollary 3.2.

Let M⁡(G)M(G) be the cycle matroid of GG represented by the incidence matrix MD⁡(G)M_{D(G)} (M⁡(G)M(G) is a regular matroid, see [30, Proposition 5.1.5]), and Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) be the regular chain group on E⁡(G)E(G) associated with MD⁡(G)M_{D(G)}. From [35], the mapping ηD⁡(C)\eta_{D(C)} defined in (2.1) is the primitive chain of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) for every cycle CC of GG, and Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is generated by {ηD⁡(C)∣C∈𝒞⁡(G)}\big\{\eta_{D(C)}\mid C\in\mathcal{C}(G)\big\}. In addition, the regular chain group Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) on E⁡(G)E(G) over ℤ\mathbb{Z} consisting of all linear combinations of rows from the matrix MD⁡(G)M_{D(G)} is exactly orthogonal to Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), i.e., Δ⁡(G)=Γ​(G)⟂\Delta(G)=\Gamma(G)^{\perp}. Again, from [35], the chain group Δ⁡(G,A)\Delta(G,A) can be generated by Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G). Then we have the following result.

Corollary 3.2.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG. Then τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) and p⁡(M⁡(G),αΓ⁡(G),ψ,k)p\big(M(G),\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi};k\big) are the same polynomial, and they satisfy that

τ⁡(G,α,k)=p⁡(M⁡(G),αΓ⁡(G),ψ,k)=|Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]|=|Δf​(G,A)|\tau(G,\alpha;k)=p\big(M(G),\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi};k\big)=|A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]|=|\Delta_{f}(G,A)|

for every Abelian group AA of order kk, every function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A satisfying αD,f=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha, and every homomorphism ψ:Γ⁡(G)→A\psi:\Gamma(G)\to A such that ψ(ηD⁡(C))=−∑e∈E⁡(G)f(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)\psi(\eta_{D(C)})=-\sum_{e\in E(G)}f(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e) for any cycle CC of GG. Furthermore, τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) has degree |V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)|V(G)|-c(G) if α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1 for any loop ee of GG and equals zero otherwise, and τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) also satisfies

τ⁡(G,α,k)={1,if E⁡(G)=∅;(k−1)​τ​(G−e,αG−e,k),if e is a bridge;α⁡(e)​τ​(G−e,αG−e,k),if e is a loop;τ⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)−τ⁡(G/e,αG/e,k),otherwise.\tau(G,\alpha;k)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $E(G)=\emptyset$};\\ (k-1)\tau(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\text{if $e$ is a bridge};\\ \alpha(e)\tau(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\text{if $e$ is a loop};\\ \tau(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)-\tau(G/e,\alpha_{G/e};k),&\text{otherwise}.\\ \end{cases}

To prove Corollary 3.2, the following lemmas are required.

Lemma 3.3.

Given a mapping f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)}. Let

Af​[G]={g∈(A−0)E⁡(G)∣g+f∈Δ⁡(G,A)}.A_{f}[G]=\big\{g\in(A-0)^{E(G)}\mid g+f\in\Delta(G,A)\big\}.

Then the mapping ϕ:Δf​(G,A)→Af​[G]\phi:\Delta_{f}(G,A)\to A_{f}[G] sending g∈Δf​(G,A)g\in\Delta_{f}(G,A) to ϕ⁡(g)=g−f\phi(g)=g-f is a bijection.

Proof.

Taking any element g∈Δf​(G,A)g\in\Delta_{f}(G,A), by g⁡(e)≠f⁡(e)g(e)\neq f(e) for all e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), then ϕ⁡(g)∈(A−0)E⁡(G)\phi(g)\in(A-0)^{E(G)} and ϕ⁡(g)+f=g∈Δf​(G,A)⊆Δ⁡(G,A)\phi(g)+f=g\in\Delta_{f}(G,A)\subseteq\Delta(G,A). Namely, ϕ\phi is well-defined. Clearly, ψ\psi is injective.

Conversely, define the mapping ϕ−1:Af​[G]→Δf​(G,A)\phi^{-1}:A_{f}[G]\to\Delta_{f}(G,A) sending g∈Af​[G]g\in A_{f}[G] to ϕ−1​(g)=g+f\phi^{-1}(g)=g+f. Given an element g∈Af​[G]g\in A_{f}[G]. Since g⁡(e)≠0g(e)\neq 0 for every e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), ϕ−1​(g)∈Δf​(G,A)\phi^{-1}(g)\in\Delta_{f}(G,A). Thus, ϕ−1\phi^{-1} is well-defined. The mapping ϕ−1\phi^{-1} is an injection obviously. Therefore, ϕ\phi is bijective. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)} and the homomorphism ψ:Γ⁡(G)→A\psi:\Gamma(G)\to A such that ψ(ηD⁡(C))=−∑e∈E⁡(G)f(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)\psi(\eta_{D(C)})=-\sum_{e\in E(G)}f(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e) for any cycle CC of GG. Then Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]=Af​[G]A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]=A_{f}[G].

Proof.

We first show Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]⊆Af​[G]A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]\subseteq A_{f}[G]. Note that the chain group Δ⁡(G,A)\Delta(G,A) is generated by the regular chain group Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) is orthogonal to Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). Then, from (3.1), this proof reduces to verifying that for any g∈Aψ​[Γ​(G)]g\in A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)], ∑e∈E⁡(G)(g+f)​(e)⋅h⁡(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(G)}(g+f)(e)\cdot h(e)=0 for all h∈Γ⁡(G)h\in\Gamma(G). Since Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is generated by {ηD⁡(C)∣C∈𝒞⁡(G)}\big\{\eta_{D(C)}\mid C\in\mathcal{C}(G)\big\}, the proof is further equivalent to checking that for any g∈Aψ​[Γ​(G)]g\in A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)],

∑e∈E⁡(G)(g+f)​(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)​(e)=0,∀C∈𝒞⁡(G).\sum_{e\in E(G)}(g+f)(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e)=0,\quad\forall\,C\in\mathcal{C}(G).

Since ∑e∈E⁡(G)g⁡(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)​(e)=ψ⁡(ηD⁡(C))\sum_{e\in E(G)}g(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e)=\psi(\eta_{D(C)}) for every g∈Aψ​[Γ​(G)]g\in A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)], it follows from ψ(ηD⁡(C))=−∑e∈E⁡(G)f(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)\psi(\eta_{D(C)})=-\sum_{e\in E(G)}f(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e) that ∑e∈E⁡(G)(g+f)​(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)​(e)\sum_{e\in E(G)}(g+f)(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e) is indeed equal to zero. This implies that g+f∈Δ⁡(G,A)g+f\in\Delta(G,A) for any g∈Aψ​[Γ​(G)]g\in A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)], that is, Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]⊆Af​[G]A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]\subseteq A_{f}[G].

For the opposite inclusion, for any g∈Af​[G]g\in A_{f}[G], we have g+f∈Δ⁡(G,A)g+f\in\Delta(G,A). Again, using (3.1), we have ∑e∈E⁡(G)(g+f)​(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(G)}(g+f)(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e)=0 for all cycles CC of GG. It follows that

∑e∈E⁡(G)g(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)=−∑e∈E⁡(G)f(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)=ψ(ηD⁡(C)).\sum_{e\in E(G)}g(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e)=-\sum_{e\in E(G)}f(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e)=\psi(\eta_{D(C)}).

This means g∈Aψ​[Γ​(G)]g\in A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)] for each g∈Af​[G]g\in A_{f}[G]. Namely, we have Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]⊇Af​[G]A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]\supseteq A_{f}[G]. Then we arrive at Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]=Af​[G]A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]=A_{f}[G]. ∎

Now we proceed to prove Corollary 3.2.

Proof of Corollary 3.2.

Note that any (A,f)(A,f)-coloring cc of GG yields an (A,f)(A,f)-tension δ​c\delta c of GG, and vice versa. We assert that for every (A,f)(A,f)-tension tt, there are exactly |A|c⁡(G)|A|^{c(G)} (A,f)(A,f)-colorings cc satisfying δ​c=t\delta c=t. Suppose tt is an (A,f)(A,f)-tension of GG satisfying t=δ​ct=\delta c for some c∈AV⁡(G)c\in A^{V(G)}. We construct a mapping c′∈AV⁡(G)c^{\prime}\in A^{V(G)} such that c′​(u)−c⁡(u)=c′​(v)−c⁡(v)c^{\prime}(u)-c(u)=c^{\prime}(v)-c(v) whenever vertices uu and vv belong to the same component of GG. It follows that c′c^{\prime} is a (A,f)(A,f)-coloring and δ​c′=t\delta c^{\prime}=t. On the other hand, if δc′′=t\delta c^{{}^{\prime\prime}}=t for another (A,f)(A,f)-coloring c′′c^{{}^{\prime\prime}}, then c′′(u)−c(u)=c′′(v)−c(v)c^{{}^{\prime\prime}}(u)-c(u)=c^{{}^{\prime\prime}}(v)-c(v) whenever uu and vv are in the same component of GG. Thus, we have shown the assertion. It follows from Theorem 2.2 that

τ⁡(G,α,k)=|Δf​(G,A)|.\tau(G,\alpha;k)=|\Delta_{f}(G,A)|. (3.3)

Applying Theorem 3.1, we have

p⁡(M⁡(G),αΓ⁡(G),ψ,k)=|Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]|.p\big(M(G),\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi};k\big)=|A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]|. (3.4)

By Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4, we obtain

|Δf​(G,A)|=|Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]|.|\Delta_{f}(G,A)|=|A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]|. (3.5)

Immediately, by integration of (3.3), (3.4) and (3.5), we arrive at

τ⁡(G,α,k)=p⁡(M⁡(G),αΓ⁡(G),ψ,k)=|Aψ​[Γ⁡(G)]|=|Δf​(G,A)|.\tau(G,\alpha;k)=p\big(M(G),\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi};k\big)=|A_{\psi}[\Gamma(G)]|=|\Delta_{f}(G,A)|.

Note that both τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) and p⁡(M⁡(G),αΓ⁡(G),ψ,k)p\big(M(G),\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi};k\big) are polynomials in kk of degree at most |V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)|V(G)|-c(G), and they agree on infinitely many positive integers kk. Hence, from the fundamental theorem of algebra, these two polynomials are the same.

In fact, we have αΓ⁡(G),ψ=αD,f=α\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi}=\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha from (2.1). In [18, Theorem 3], it is stated that

a homogeneous assigning α of M⁡(G) is proper ⟺ α⁡(e)=1 for each loop e of M⁡(G).\text{a homogeneous assigning $\alpha$ of $M(G)$ is proper $\Longleftrightarrow$ $\alpha(e)=1$ for each loop $e$ of $M(G)$}.

Together with Theorem 3.1 and r⁡(M⁡(G))=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)r\big(M(G)\big)=|V(G)|-c(G), we have that τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) has degree |V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)|V(G)|-c(G) if α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1 for any loop ee of GG and equals zero otherwise. Finally, the remaining part is a direct result of Theorem 2.5 via τ⁡(G,α,k)=k−c⁡(G)​P​(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k)=k^{-c(G)}P(G,\alpha;k). ∎

In [15, Proposition 2.2], it is demonstrated that f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)} is a tension of GG if and only if ff satisfies the condition ∑e∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0 for every cycle CC of GG. It follows that αD,f≡0\alpha_{D,f}\equiv 0 for every f∈Δ⁡(G,A)f\in\Delta(G,A). So, the assigning polynomial τ⁡(G,αD,f,k)\tau(G,\alpha_{D,f};k) is the classical tension polynomial of GG (see [15]) whenever f∈Δ⁡(G,A)f\in\Delta(G,A).

Let MM be a matroid on the ground set EE and ≺\prec be a linear ordering on EE. For every subset X⊆EX\subseteq E, the notation min⁡(X){\rm min}(X) represents the minimal element of XX with respect to ≺\prec. A subset X⊆EX\subseteq E is (M,≺)(M,\prec)-compatible if C∩X≠{min⁡(C)}C\cap X\neq\{{\rm min}(C)\} for each C∈𝒞⁡(M)C\in\mathcal{C}(M), where 𝒞⁡(M)\mathcal{C}(M) is the set of all circuits of MM. Furthermore, we use ℰ⁡(M,≺)\mathcal{E}(M,\prec) to denote the collection of all (M∗,≺)(M^{*},\prec)-compatible subsets of EE, where M∗M^{*} is the dual matroid of MM. For any X⊆EX\subseteq E and assigning α\alpha of MM, we define δ⁡(M,α,X)\delta(M,\alpha;X) to be

δ⁡(M,α,X)=:{0,if there exists C∈𝒞⁡(M) such that C⊆X and α⁡(C)=1;1,otherwise.\delta(M,\alpha;X)=:\begin{cases}0,&\text{if there exists $C\in\mathcal{C}(M)$ such that $C\subseteq X$ and $\alpha(C)=1$};\\ 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

For a regular matroid MM, Kochol derived an explicit expression for the α\alpha-assigning polynomial p⁡(M,α,k)p(M,\alpha;k) over all (M∗,≺)(M^{*},\prec)-compatible subsets of EE in [18, Theorem 2].

Theorem 3.5 ([18], Theorem 2).

Let α\alpha be a homogeneous assigning of a regular matroid MM on EE and ≺\prec be a linear ordering of EE. Then,

p⁡(M,α,k)=∑X∈ℰ⁡(M,≺)δ⁡(M,α,X)​(−1)|X|​(k−1)r⁡(M/X).p(M,\alpha;k)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{E}(M,\prec)}\delta(M,\alpha;X)(-1)^{|X|}(k-1)^{r(M/X)}.

A bond of a graph is a minimal nonempty edge cut, which is the smallest nonempty subset of edges whose removal from the graph results in an increase in the number of components. Below we return to the cycle matroid M⁡(G)M(G) on E⁡(G)E(G) represented by MD⁡(G)M_{D(G)}. Its dual matroid M∗​(G)M^{*}(G), also on E⁡(G)E(G), is referred to as a bond matroid of GG (GG may be not a planar graph). In [30, Proposition 2.3.1], it is demonstrated that

X⊆E⁡(G) is a circuit of M∗​(G) if and only if X is a bond of G.\text{$X\subseteq E(G)$ is a circuit of $M^{*}(G)$ if and only if $X$ is a bond of $G$}.

Let ≺\prec be a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). Define ℰ⁡(G,≺)\mathcal{E}(G,\prec) as

ℰ⁡(G,≺):={X⊆E⁡(G)∣X∩C∗≠{min⁡(C∗)}​ for all bonds C∗ of G}.\mathcal{E}(G,\prec):=\big\{X\subseteq E(G)\mid X\cap C^{*}\neq\{{\rm min}(C^{*})\}\text{ for all bonds $C^{*}$ of $G$}\big\}.

It follows that

ℰ⁡(G,≺)=ℰ⁡(M⁡(G),≺).\mathcal{E}(G,\prec)=\mathcal{E}\big(M(G),\prec\big). (3.6)

For any X⊆E⁡(G)X\subseteq E(G) and assigning α\alpha of GG, we define δ⁡(G,α,X)\delta(G,\alpha;X) by

δ⁡(G,α,X)=:{0,if there exists C∈𝒞⁡(G) such that E⁡(C)⊆X and α⁡(C)=1;1,otherwise.\delta(G,\alpha;X)=:\begin{cases}0,&\text{if there exists $C\in\mathcal{C}(G)$ such that $E(C)\subseteq X$ and $\alpha(C)=1$};\\ 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

From (2.1), every admissible assigning α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f} of GG induced by f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)} is precisely a homogeneous assigning αΓ⁡(G),ψ\alpha_{\Gamma(G),\psi} of M⁡(G)M(G), where the homomorphism ψ:Γ⁡(G)→A\psi:\Gamma(G)\to A satisfies ψ(ηD⁡(C))=−∑e∈E⁡(G)f(e)⋅ηD⁡(C)(e)\psi(\eta_{D(C)})=-\sum_{e\in E(G)}f(e)\cdot\eta_{D(C)}(e) for any cycle CC of GG. In this sense, we have

δ⁡(G,α,X)=δ⁡(M⁡(G),α,X), for every ​X⊆E⁡(G).\delta(G,\alpha;X)=\delta\big(M(G),\alpha;X\big),\quad\text{ for every }X\subseteq E(G). (3.7)

By integrating the preceding discussions, as a direct consequence of Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 3.5, we conclude an analogous result of Theorem 3.5 concerning τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) and P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in the following corollary.

Corollary 3.6.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG and ≺\prec a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). Then

τ⁡(G,α,k)=∑X∈ℰ⁡(G,≺)δ⁡(G,α,X)​(−1)|X|​(k−1)r⁡(G)−r⁡(X)\tau(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{E}(G,\prec)}\delta(G,\alpha;X)(-1)^{|X|}(k-1)^{r(G)-r(X)}

and

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑X∈ℰ⁡(G,≺)δ⁡(G,α,X)​(−1)|X|​(k−1)c⁡(G|X),P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{E}(G,\prec)}\delta(G,\alpha;X)(-1)^{|X|}(k-1)^{c(G|X)},

where rr is the rank function of GG given by r⁡(X):=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G|X)r(X):=|V(G)|-c(G|X) for X⊆E⁡(G)X\subseteq E(G).

Proof.

Suppose α\alpha is equal to the admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} for some f∈AE⁡(G)f\in A^{E(G)}. Together with the relations in (3.6) and (3.7), by using Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 3.5, we have

τ⁡(G,α,k)=∑X∈ℰ⁡(G,≺)δ⁡(G,α,X)​(−1)|X|​(k−1)r⁡(M⁡(G)/X).\tau(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{E}(G,\prec)}\delta(G,\alpha;X)(-1)^{|X|}(k-1)^{r(M(G)/X)}.

Note that r⁡(M⁡(G)/X)=r⁡(M⁡(G))−rM⁡(G)​(X)r\big(M(G)/X\big)=r\big(M(G)\big)-r_{M(G)}(X) from [30, Proposition 3.1.6], where rM⁡(G)r_{M(G)} is the rank function of M⁡(G)M(G). It follows from rM⁡(G)​(X)=r​(X)r_{M(G)}(X)=r(X) for any X⊆E⁡(G)X\subseteq E(G) that

τ⁡(G,α,k)=∑X∈ℰ⁡(G,≺)δ⁡(G,α,X)​(−1)|X|​(k−1)r⁡(G)−r⁡(X).\tau(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{E}(G,\prec)}\delta(G,\alpha;X)(-1)^{|X|}(k-1)^{r(G)-r(X)}.

Combining the relations r⁡(X)=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G|X)r(X)=|V(G)|-c(G|X) and P⁡(G,α,k)=kc⁡(G)​τ​(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=k^{c(G)}\tau(G,\alpha;k), we derive the second formula in Corollary 3.6. ∎

4 Generalization of Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem

A natural question is whether there is a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials. To address this, we introduce the concept of a broken α\alpha-compatible cycle as an extension of the usual broken cycle proposed by Whitney [36].

Definition 4.1.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and ≺\prec be a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). A subgraph HH of GG is said to be:

  • •

    an α\alpha-compatible cycle of GG if HH is a cycle and α⁡(H)=0\alpha(H)=0;

  • •

    a broken α\alpha-compatible cycle of GG if HH is obtained from an α\alpha-compatible cycle by removing the maximal element with respect to the linear ordering ≺\prec.

The following result provides a counting interpretation for the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) via broken α\alpha-compatible cycle, extending the Whitney’s celebrated Broken Cycle Theorem [36]. It is worth noting that the coefficients wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) in Theorem 4.2 are independent of the choice of edge order.

Theorem 4.2 (Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem).

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG and ≺\prec a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). Write P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G,α)​k|V⁡(G)|−iP(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G,\alpha)k^{|V(G)|-i}. Then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that have exactly ii edges and do not contain broken α\alpha-compatible cycles with respect to ≺\prec.

Proof.

Let E(G)={em≺⋯≺e2≺e1}E(G)=\{e_{m}\prec\cdots\prec e_{2}\prec e_{1}\}. We prove the result by induction on mm. If m=0m=0, there is nothing to prove. Suppose m≥1m\geq 1 and the result holds for smaller values of mm. Let em=u​ve_{m}=uv. If eme_{m} is a loop and α⁡(em)=0\alpha(e_{m})=0, it is trivial via Theorem 2.5. If eme_{m} is a loop and α⁡(em)=1\alpha(e_{m})=1, from

P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)

in Theorem 2.5, the result holds in this case by the inductive hypothesis.

If eme_{m} is a link, by the inductive hypothesis, the result holds for both graphs G−emG-e_{m} and G/emG/e_{m}. With a slight abuse of notation, we identify E(G/em)={em−1≺⋯≺e2≺e1}E(G/e_{m})=\{e_{m-1}\prec\cdots\prec e_{2}\prec e_{1}\}. More specifically, by identifying the ends of eme_{m}, this create a single new vertex of G/emG/e_{m}, denoted by vemv_{e_{m}}. Suppose the edge ei=x​ye_{i}=xy in GG for some i<mi<m. If neither xx nor yy is one of the vertices uu or vv, then eie_{i} automatically remains an edge in G/emG/e_{m}. If either xx or yy is one of the vertices uu or vv, we identity eie_{i} as u​vemuv_{e_{m}}, vem​vv_{e_{m}}v or vem​vemv_{e_{m}}v_{e_{m}} depending on the incidence of eie_{i} in GG. By the Deletion-contraction Formula in Theorem 2.5, we have w0​(G,α)=w0​(G−em,αG−em)w_{0}(G,\alpha)=w_{0}(G-e_{m},\alpha_{G-e_{m}}) and

wi(G,α)=wi(G−em,αG−em)+wi−1(G/em,αG/em),i=1,2,…,r(G).w_{i}(G,\alpha)=w_{i}(G-e_{m},\alpha_{G-e_{m}})+w_{i-1}(G/e_{m},\alpha_{G/e_{m}}),\;i=1,2,\ldots,r(G). (4.1)

Therefore, to complete the induction step, it is sufficient to check that the relation in (4.1) is true. But this is a consequence of the following two simple facts: (a) HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG that does not contain ee and broken α\alpha-compatible cycles if and only if HH is an αG−em\alpha_{G-e_{m}}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−emG-e_{m} that does not contain broken αG−em\alpha_{G-e_{m}}-compatible cycles; (b) HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG that contains ee and no broken α\alpha-compatible cycles if and only if H/emH/e_{m} is an αG/em\alpha_{G/e_{m}}-compatible spanning subgraph of G/emG/e_{m} that does not contain broken αG/em\alpha_{G/e_{m}}-compatible cycles. ∎

In the remainder of this section, we present a direct proof of Theorem 4.2. For this purpose, the next lemma is required.

Lemma 4.3.

Let α\alpha be a DD-admissible assigning of GG and ≺\prec a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). Suppose HH is a subgraph of GG containing a broken α\alpha-compatible cycle BB and B=C−eCB=C-e_{C} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle CC of GG, where eCe_{C} is the maximal member in E⁡(C)E(C) with respect to ≺\prec. If HH is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG and eC∉E⁡(H)e_{C}\notin E(H), then H+eCH+e_{C} is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph.

Proof.

Note that CC is a cycle in H+eCH+e_{C}, but not in HH. If H+eCH+e_{C} contains exactly one more cycle CC than HH, there is nothing left to prove. Otherwise, H+eCH+e_{C} contains at least one additional cycle compared to HH, excluding the cycle CC. Every such additional cycle, together with the cycle CC, forms a theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C}. Therefore, this case reduces to verifying that each such the theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C} is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG. Without loss of generality, we only need to examine the following oriented theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C} with the orientation DD, as shown in Figure 1.

More specifically, in Figure 1, the edge eC=u0​v0e_{C}=u_{0}v_{0}; the cycle CC, which is the union of the red directed path P1=(ui,ui−1,…,vk−1,vk)P_{1}=(u_{i},u_{i-1},\ldots,v_{k-1},v_{k}) and the green directed path P2=(vk,vk+1,…,vl,ui)P_{2}=(v_{k},v_{k+1},\ldots,v_{l},u_{i}), and the cycle C1C_{1}, which is the union of the red directed path P1P_{1} and the blue directed path P3=(ui,ui+1,…,uj,vk)P_{3}=(u_{i},u_{i+1},\ldots,u_{j},v_{k}), are in H+eCH+e_{C} but not in HH; the cycle C2C_{2} is the common cycle of H+eCH+e_{C} and HH, formed by the union of both directed paths P2P_{2} and P3P_{3}. Then, to complete our proof, it suffices to show α⁡(C)=α⁡(C1)=α⁡(C2)=0\alpha(C)=\alpha(C_{1})=\alpha(C_{2})=0.

Since α\alpha is DD-admissible, we may assume α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f} for some Abelian group AA and function f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A. Combining that CC and HH are α\alpha-compatible subgraphs of GG, this means

αD,f​(C)=α⁡(C)=0 and αD,f​(C2)=α⁡(C2)=0.\alpha_{D,f}(C)=\alpha(C)=0\quad\mbox{\rm~and~}\quad\alpha_{D,f}(C_{2})=\alpha(C_{2})=0.

This is further equivalent to satisfying the following equations

∑e∈E⁡(C)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P1)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P2)ηD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(C)}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{1})}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{2})}\eta_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0

and

∑e∈E⁡(C2)ηD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P2)ηD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P3)ηD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)=0.\sum_{e\in E(C_{2})}\eta_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{2})}\eta_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{3})}\eta_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)=0.

Taking the clockwise as the reference direction for every cycle, then ηD⁡(C1)​(e)=−ηD⁡(C)​(e)\eta_{D(C_{1})}(e)=-\eta_{D(C)}(e) for any edge e∈E⁡(P1)e\in E(P_{1}) and ηD⁡(C1)​(e)=ηD⁡(C2)​(e)\eta_{D(C_{1})}(e)=\eta_{D(C_{2})}(e) for any edge e∈E⁡(P3)e\in E(P_{3}). Thus, we deduce

∑e∈E⁡(C1)ηD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P1)ηD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P3)ηD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)=0.\sum_{e\in E(C_{1})}\eta_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{1})}\eta_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{3})}\eta_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)=0.

This implies α⁡(C1)=αD,f​(C1)=0\alpha(C_{1})=\alpha_{D,f}(C_{1})=0. Therefore, H+eCH+e_{C} is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG. ∎

We now return to the proof of the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Suppose GG has q≥0q\geq 0 broken α\alpha-compatible cycles. For every broken α\alpha-compatible cycle BB, let eBe_{B} be the maximal member in BB with respect to the linear ordering ≺\prec. We can arrange the broken α\alpha-compatible cycles B1,…,BqB_{1},\ldots,B_{q} such that eB1⪯eB2⋯⪯eBqe_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}}\cdots\preceq e_{B_{q}}. Let 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing the broken α\alpha-compatible cycle B1B_{1}. For i=2,…,qi=2,\ldots,q, let 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing the broken α\alpha-compatible cycle BiB_{i} but not any of B1,…,Bi−1B_{1},\ldots,B_{i-1}. In addition, let 𝒮q+1\mathcal{S}_{q+1} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing no broken α\alpha-compatible cycles. Then {𝒮1,𝒮2,…,𝒮q+1}\{\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{q+1}\} decomposes the set of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG. Combining Theorem 2.2, the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) can be written in the form

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=1q+1∑H∈𝒮i(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=1}^{q+1}\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}. (4.2)

We first consider 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. Assume B1=C1−eC1B_{1}=C_{1}-e_{C_{1}} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle C1C_{1} of GG, where eC1e_{C_{1}} is the maximal member in C1C_{1} with respect to ≺\prec. Clearly each member HH in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}} gives rise to a unique member H−eC1H-e_{C_{1}} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} that does not contain eC1e_{C_{1}}. Conversely, according to Lemma 4.3, each member HH in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing no eC1e_{C_{1}} gives rise to a unique member H+eC1H+e_{C_{1}} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}}. In addition, since B1+eC1=C1B_{1}+e_{C_{1}}=C_{1} is a cycle of GG, for each H∈𝒮1H\in\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}}, we have c⁡(H)=c⁡(H−eC1)c(H)=c(H-e_{C_{1}}). Thus, we derive

∑H∈𝒮1,eC1∈E⁡(H)((−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)+(−1)|E⁡(H)|−1​kc⁡(H−eC1))=0.\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{1},\,e_{C_{1}}\in E(H)}\big((-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}+(-1)^{|E(H)|-1}k^{c(H-e_{C_{1}})}\big)=0.

Namely, we arrive at ∑H∈𝒮1(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}=0 in (4.2).

Consider 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}. Assume B2=C2−eC2B_{2}=C_{2}-e_{C_{2}} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle C2C_{2} of GG, where eC2e_{C_{2}} is the maximal member in C2C_{2} with respect to ≺\prec. It follows from the ordering eB1⪯eB2e_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}} that eB1⪯eB2≺eC2e_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}}\prec e_{C_{2}}. So, B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} do not contain eC2e_{C_{2}}. Combining this, using the same argument as the case 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, we conclude that every element HH in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} containing no eC2e_{C_{2}} gives rise to a unique member H+eC2H+e_{C_{2}} in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} containing eC2e_{C_{2}}, and vice versa. Hence, we also obtain ∑H∈𝒮2(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}=0 in (4.2).

Likewise, we can deduce the total contribution of the members in 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} to P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is zero for each i=1,2,…,qi=1,2,\ldots,q. Therefore, P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in (4.2) can be written as

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑H∈𝒮q+1(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}. (4.3)

Since every element H∈𝒮q+1H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1} is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG and contains no broken α\alpha-compatible cycles, we can deduce that HH contains no cycles. Therefore, HH is a forest. This implies that for any member H∈𝒮q+1H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1},

|E⁡(H)|≤r⁡(G) and c⁡(H)=|V⁡(G)|−|E⁡(H)|.|E(H)|\leq r(G)\quad\mbox{\rm~and~}\quad c(H)=|V(G)|-|E(H)|.

Thus, P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in (4.3) can be further simplified to the following form

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G,α)​k|V⁡(G)|−i,P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G,\alpha)k^{|V(G)|-i},

which completes the proof. ∎

As an immediate result of Theorem 4.2, we have the next corollary.

Corollary 4.4.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG. Then (−1)|V⁡(G)|​P​(G,α,−1)(-1)^{|V(G)|}P(G,\alpha;-1) is the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain broken α\alpha-compatible cycles with respect to a linear ordering ≺\prec on E⁡(G)E(G).

Notably, the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) agrees with the chromatic polynomial P⁡(G,k)P(G;k) of GG whenever GG is α\alpha-compatible. When GG is α\alpha-compatible, the α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph, α\alpha-compatible cycle and broken α\alpha-compatible cycle of GG correspond to the ordinary spanning subgraph, cycle and broken cycle of GG, respectively. Hence, Theorem 4.2 deduces the following Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem in [36] directly.

Theorem 4.5 ([36]).

Write the chromatic polynomial as P⁡(G,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G)​k|V⁡(G)|−iP(G;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G)k^{|V(G)|-i}. Then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G)w_{i}(G) is the number of spanning subgraphs of GG that have exactly ii edges and do not contain broken cycles with respect to a linear ordering ≺\prec on E⁡(G)E(G).

5 Coefficient comparisons and further explorations

In this section, we primarily apply the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem to explore how the coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials vary with changes in admissible assignings and to handle certain group coloring problems in graphs. We first establish a unified order-preserving relation from admissible assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials when both are naturally ordered. Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and ≺\prec be a linear ordering on E⁡(G)E(G). For convenience, we denote by 𝒞⁡(G,α)\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha), 𝒞′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha) and 𝒞′′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha) the sets of α\alpha-compatible cycles, broken α\alpha-compatible cycles, and α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain broken α\alpha-compatible cycles with respect to ≺\prec, respectively.

Theorem 5.1 (Comparison of Coefficients).

Let α,α′\alpha,\alpha^{\prime} be two admissible assignings of GG. If α⁡(C)≤α′​(C)\alpha(C)\leq\alpha^{\prime}(C) for all cycles C∈𝒞⁡(G)C\in\mathcal{C}(G), then the unsigned coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomials P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) and P⁡(G,α′,k)P(G,\alpha^{\prime};k) satisfy

wi​(G,α)≤wi​(G,α′) for i=0,1,…,r⁡(G).w_{i}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{i}(G,\alpha^{\prime})\quad\mbox{ for }\quad i=0,1,\ldots,r(G).

In particular, wi​(G)=wi​(G,0)≤wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G)=w_{i}(G,0)\leq w_{i}(G,\alpha) for any admissible assigning α\alpha of GG.

Proof.

By Theorem 4.2, the proof reduces to showing that every member HH of 𝒞′′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha) belongs to 𝒞′′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). Given an element H∈𝒞′′​(G,α)H\in\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha). As HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no broken α\alpha-compatible cycles, this implies that HH does not contain cycles. Furthermore, since α⁡(C)≤α′​(C)\alpha(C)\leq\alpha^{\prime}(C) for any cycle CC of GG, we have 𝒞⁡(G,α)⊇𝒞⁡(G,α′)\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha)\supseteq\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). This means 𝒞′​(G,α)⊇𝒞′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha)\supseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). This further deduces that HH does not contain broken α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible cycles. Therefore, we conclude that HH is an α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no broken α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible cycles. Namely, 𝒞′′​(G,α)⊆𝒞′′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha)\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). ∎

When GG is a loopless graph, each unsigned coefficient wi​(G)w_{i}(G) of P⁡(G,k)P(G;k) is a positive integer, which is easily obtained from Theorem 4.5. Applying Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 5.1 to this, we derive that for any admissible assigning α\alpha, the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) are nonzero and alternate in sign, unless α⁡(e)=0\alpha(e)=0 for some loop ee.

Corollary 5.2.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigining of GG. Then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is a positive integer, unless α⁡(e)=0\alpha(e)=0 for some loop ee of GG. Moreover, w0​(G,α)=1w_{0}(G,\alpha)=1 whenever P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is not the zero polynomial.

According to the relationship P⁡(G,α,k)=kc⁡(G)​τ​(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=k^{c(G)}\tau(G,\alpha;k), it is worth noting that for any admissible assigning α\alpha, the coefficients of the α\alpha-assigning polynomial τ⁡(G,α,k)\tau(G,\alpha;k) share the same properties as those of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k), as outlined in Theorem 2.6, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.4, Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.2.

It is well-known that the unimodality of the sequence wi​(G)w_{i}(G) was conjectured by Read [31], and the log-concavity was conjectured by Hoggar [11]. Both of these conjectures have been confirmed by Huh et al. [1, 12, 13]. Inspired by their work, we conjecture that the unsigned coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) form a log-concave, and hence unimodal, sequence for all graphs GG and almost all admissible assignings of GG.

Conjecture 5.3.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG such that α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1 for all loops ee of GG. Then the sequence w0​(G,α),w1​(G,α),…,wr⁡(G)​(G,α)w_{0}(G,\alpha),w_{1}(G,\alpha),\ldots,w_{r(G)}(G,\alpha) satisfies the following properties:

  • •

    The sequence wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is unimodal, i.e., there is an index 0≤j≤r⁡(G)0\leq j\leq r(G) such that

    w0​(G,α)≤⋯≤wj−1​(G,α)≤wj​(G,α)≥wj+1​(G,α)≥⋯≥wr⁡(G)​(G,α).w_{0}(G,\alpha)\leq\cdots\leq w_{j-1}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{j}(G,\alpha)\geq w_{j+1}(G,\alpha)\geq\cdots\geq w_{r(G)}(G,\alpha).
  • •

    The sequence wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is log-concave, i.e, for j=1,…,r⁡(G)−1j=1,\ldots,r(G)-1,

    wj−1​(G,α)​wj+1​(G,α)≤wj​(G,α)2.w_{j-1}(G,\alpha)w_{j+1}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{j}(G,\alpha)^{2}.

It is a pleasant surprise that the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem provides a new perspective on addressing certain group coloring problems in graphs. A well-known property in [33] says that if a graph has a nowhere-zero AA-flow, then it admits a nowhere-zero A′A^{\prime}-flow for any Abelian group A′A^{\prime} whose order is at least the order of AA. This does not extend to the more general concept of group connectivity observed by Jaeger et al. [14]. For a connected planar graph GG, Jaeger et al. [14] also showed that GG is AA-colorable if and only if the dual graph G∗G^{*} is AA-connected. Naturally, there is a corresponding problem in group colorings: for any Abelian groups A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} with the same order, is a A1A_{1}-colorable graph also A2A_{2}-colorable?

Most recently, Langhede and Thomassen in [26] confirmed that the property holds if A′A^{\prime} is sufficiently large compared to AA. This further implied that GG is always AA-colorable whenever AA has a sufficiently large order, which can be explained by the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem. More specifically, note the basic fact that for a loopless graph GG, GG is AA-colorable for some Abelian group AA if and only if P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)>0P\big(D(G),f;A\big)>0 for any f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A. This is also equivalent to saying that GG is AA-colorable if and only if P⁡(G,αD,f,|A|)>0P(G,\alpha_{D,f};|A|)>0 for any DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} related to f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A. When GG is a loopless graph, it follows from Theorem 4.2 that w0​(G,α)=1w_{0}(G,\alpha)=1 for any admissible assigning α\alpha of GG. Thus, P⁡(G,α,|A|)>0P(G,\alpha;|A|)>0 holds for all admissible assignings α\alpha of GG in this case whenever the Abelian group AA has a large enough order.

We conclude this section with the next corollary, summarizing the above findings.

Corollary 5.4.

Let A,A′A,A^{\prime} be two Abelian groups of the same order, GG be a A′A^{\prime}-colorable graph and D,D′D,D^{\prime} be two orientations. If each DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} of GG with f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A is a D′D^{\prime}-admissible assigning αD′,f′\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}} of GG for some f′:E⁡(G)→A′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to A^{\prime}, then GG is AA-colorable.

Proof.

Since GG is A′A^{\prime}-colorable, we have P⁡(D′​(G),f′,A′)>0P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};A^{\prime}\big)>0 for any f′:E⁡(G)→A′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to A^{\prime}. As each DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} with f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A is a D′D^{\prime}-admissible assigning αD′,f′\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}} of GG for some f′:E⁡(G)→A′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to A^{\prime}, it follows that for any f:E⁡(G)→Af:E(G)\to A,

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,A)=P⁡(G,α,|A|)=P⁡(D′​(G),f′,A′)>0P\big(D(G),f;A\big)=P(G,\alpha;|A|)=P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};A^{\prime}\big)>0

via Corollary 2.3, where α=αD,f=αD′,f′\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}}. This implies that GG is AA-colorable. ∎
